summary: Describes a secure binding between the multiple addresses with different prefixes that a host has at a multihomed site. It uses Cryptographically Generated Addresses or a variant with the same format, so that the addresses can be verified as belonging together.

eli5.summary: One person with several home addresses needs to prove they are really the same person. This note ties the addresses together with math so nobody can fake it.

questions: how are multihomed ipv6 addresses bound securely
how does hba differ from cga
subtitle: Addresses that carry a hash of the host's other prefixes, so a peer can check they belong together.

tldr.problem: A multihomed IPv6 host has one address per ISP prefix, and switching a live communication between them invites redirection attacks unless the addresses are securely bound together.
tldr.mechanism: The host builds each interface identifier as a hash of a random modifier, the prefix and the whole prefix set, reusing the Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA) format, so one hash lets a peer verify that another address belongs to the same set.
tldr.outcome: HBAs protect against communication hijacking and time shifting attacks without public key operations for every communication, but they cannot stop man-in-the-middle attacks or flooding of a prefix, and the prefix set is fixed when the set is generated.

today: RFC 5535 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It supplies the secure address binding that Shim6 (RFC 5533) uses.

sections.title: Why Multihomed Hosts Need Bound Addresses
sections.content:
IPv6 sites get addresses from their ISPs, which keeps the global routing tables small. A multihomed site therefore has several prefixes, one per ISP, and a communication that must survive a change of ISP has to change the address it uses. That exposes it to attacks, so the addresses need a secure binding.

This RFC describes Hash-Based Addresses (HBAs), a tool against some of those attacks, in particular future or premeditated attacks, also called time shifting attacks. Unlike a mobile node, a host in a multihomed site usually knows its set of addresses in advance, and HBAs take advantage of that stability. They use only symmetric key cryptography and have smaller computational requirements than CGAs, which use public key cryptography and can deal with changing address sets.
sections.eli5: If you move house but keep your name, people want proof that the new house really is yours. HBAs give that proof ahead of time.

sections.title: The Core Idea
sections.content:
The basic goal is to bind together the IPv6 addresses of one multihomed host. Say the prefixes are A, B, C and D. The host makes a prefix list P and a random Modifier M, then builds each address as the prefix followed by a hash of M, that prefix and P. Given one valid address, P and M, anyone can check whether another address is in the group with a single hash operation.

The design follows several motivations: avoid trusted third parties such as repositories or a public key infrastructure because of deployment cost; use routable IPv6 addresses as identifiers, so the security information goes into the interface identifier; and avoid public key operations for every communication. HBA and CGA are not mutually exclusive, and an address can be both.

The threat model covers redirection attacks. HBAs give full protection against communication hijacking, while flooding attacks are handled by Shim6 itself.
sections.eli5: Every address in the family has a stamp that depends on all the other addresses. Change the family and every stamp changes.

sections.title: Compatibility with CGAs
sections.content:
HBAs are built to be compatible with Cryptographically Generated Addresses (RFC 3972), so that nodes can keep using Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971) and so that CGAs can add a feature HBAs lack: adding new prefixes after the set is generated. HBA uses a CGA extension field, the Multi-Prefix extension, to carry the prefix set.

Three kinds of address result. CGA-only addresses lack the extension and are bound to a public key and one prefix. CGA/HBA addresses include the extension and are bound to a public key and a prefix set. HBA-only addresses are bound to a prefix set and carry a random nonce in the Public Key field instead of a key, so they cannot be used for SeND.
sections.eli5: HBAs reuse the same address layout as an older scheme so that existing tools keep working. Some addresses carry a lock-and-key, some only the family stamp, some both.

sections.title: The Multi-Prefix Extension
sections.content:
The Multi-Prefix extension is a type-length-value structure using the CGA extension format from RFC 4581. It has a 16-bit Extension Type, a 16-bit Extension Data Length, a P flag that is set when a public key is included, a 31-bit Reserved field that MUST be zero, and a vector of 64-bit prefixes, Prefix[1] to Prefix[n].

IANA assigned it CGA Extension Type value 0x0012.
sections.eli5: It is a list printed inside the address recipe saying which prefixes belong to the family.

sections.title: Generating an HBA Set
sections.content:
Generation is a sequence of lightly modified CGA generations from RFC 3972, valid for Sec values 0, 1 and 2. The inputs are a vector of 64-bit prefixes, a Sec value and, optionally, a public key. Without a key, a random 384-bit value is encoded as an RSA key structure so that the result still looks like a CGA.

The steps: build the Multi-Prefix extension with Ext Len equal to n*8 + 4; generate a random 128-bit Modifier; hash it with SHA-1 together with nine zero octets, the key and the extension, keeping the leftmost 112 bits as Hash2; and repeat with an incremented Modifier until the leftmost 16*Sec bits of Hash2 are zero. Then, for each prefix, hash the final Modifier, the prefix, a collision count, the key and the extension, keep the leftmost 64 bits, write Sec into the three leftmost bits, clear the u and g bits, and prepend the prefix. After three duplicate address detection collisions, the process stops and reports an error.
sections.eli5: The host mixes a secret random number with each prefix and the whole list, makes a short fingerprint, and uses that fingerprint as the second half of each address.

sections.title: Verifying that an Address Belongs to the Set
sections.content:
A properly formed HBA passes ordinary CGA verification against its own parameter data structure. For multihoming, a receiver must also check that a different address belongs to the set defined by another address's structure. That would fail plain CGA verification because the prefix would not match, so the receiver first checks that the new address's prefix is in the Multi-Prefix extension and then substitutes that prefix into the Subnet Prefix field.

It then runs the CGA verification steps: check the collision count is 0, 1 or 2, hash the structure, compare the leftmost 64 bits with the interface identifier (ignoring the three leftmost bits and the u and g bits), read Sec, and check that the leftmost 16*Sec bits of Hash2 are zero.
sections.eli5: To check a new address, the receiver redoes the fingerprint with the new prefix. If it matches, the address is in the family.

sections.title: An Example with Shim6
sections.content:
A site has two providers, ISPA and ISPB. Host1 generates an HBA set from both prefixes and a public key, giving two addresses with their parameter data structures. It talks to Host2 using the first address. When one of the hosts wants multihoming support, the Shim6 Host-Pair Context exchange sends the parameter data structure to Host2, which verifies it against the address in use.

If the path through ISPA fails, Host1 tells Host2 about the address from ISPB. Host2 runs HBA verification and, since the prefix is in the Multi-Prefix extension, accepts it. Packets then use the new address while the original remains the identifier for upper layers. Further packets need no more HBA verification.

If a new prefix appears after renumbering, it is not in the set. Host1 can then sign a Shim6 UPDATE with the private key, using the CGA capability. In the long run the site must regenerate its HBA sets, and all addresses change, because the prefix set is an input to every one.
sections.eli5: When the main road closes, the host says 'use my other house'. The friend checks the family stamp and, if it matches, switches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With HBAs, a node using address A can redirect a communication to B if and only if B is in the same HBA set. An attacker would have to find a parameter structure whose set contains both addresses, which takes brute force of about O(2^59) generations because 59 of the 64 interface identifier bits are hash bits. A non-zero Sec raises this to O(2^(59+16*Sec)).

HBAs cannot prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, but they do protect against time shifting attacks: an attacker who must also change the prefix set has to stay on path permanently. They do not fully prevent flooding; targeting a specific address is infeasible, but flooding a prefix is possible, so additional mechanisms such as reachability tests are required.

The RFC also notes that temporary addresses cost more when Sec is above zero, that the analysis in RFC 4982 found CGAs and their extensions unaffected by recent attacks on hash functions, and that holding HBA state can be a DoS vector, which the Shim6 4-way handshake mitigates.
sections.eli5: Faking a matching stamp would take an impossibly long time. But a bad guy standing in the middle of the road the whole time can still meddle.
